prompt: What range of values does an `int8` hold?
hint: Eight bits, one of them spent on the sign.

choices.why: That is `uint8`, which gives up the negative numbers.

choices.text: −127 to 127, the same distance each way
choices.why: The range is not symmetric: zero takes one of the 256 values, and the extra one goes to the negative side.
Right. `go doc math.MaxInt` printed `MinInt8` as −128 and `MaxInt8` as 127.
That would need nine bits. Eight bits make 256 values in all, split across both signs.

prompt: On the lab's amd64 the program printed `int is 64 bits`. What did the same source print when built with `GOARCH=386`?
hint: 386 is 32-bit x86.

choices.text: `int is 64 bits`, because an `int` is 64 bits wherever Go runs
choices.why: That is `int64`. Plain `int` follows the platform, which is why `MaxInt` says "depending on intSize".
Right, and the largest `int` it printed was 2147483647.
No platform Go supports in the lab's run gave 16; the 32-bit build printed 32.

choices.text: Nothing: the build fails, because `int` has no size on 386
choices.why: It built and ran. `int` always has a size; the size depends on the platform.

prompt: `var small int8 = 127`, then `small++`, then `fmt.Println(small)`. What happens?
hint: The addition happens while the program runs.

choices.why: 128 does not fit in an `int8`, whose largest value is 127.

choices.text: It prints `-128`, having wrapped round past the top
choices.why: Right. Run-time overflow wraps around to the smallest value, silently.

choices.text: It panics with an overflow error
choices.why: Go panics on an integer divided by zero, not on overflow. Overflow wraps with no message.
The compiler refuses constants that do not fit; a variable's value is not known to it.

prompt: A program keeps the number of retries left in `var left uint = 2` and, by mistake, runs `left -= 3`. What does `left` hold now?
hint: An unsigned type has no −1 to land on.

choices.why: A `uint` cannot hold a negative number; that is the whole difference from `int`.

choices.text: 0, because an unsigned value stops at zero
choices.why: Nothing in Go stops at the edge. Integer arithmetic wraps, in both directions.
Right. 2 − 3 wraps round to the top, as `0 − 1` did in the section.

choices.text: Nothing: the program panics at the subtraction
choices.why: Overflow is silent in Go; only dividing an integer by zero panics among these operations.

prompt: How many different values can an `int16` hold, counting zero?
hint: Sixteen bits, each 0 or 1.

prompt: What does `fmt.Println(-17 / 5, -17 % 5)` print?
hint: Truncated toward zero; the remainder keeps the sign of −17.

choices.why: That is a language that rounds down, as Python does. Go truncates toward zero.
The quotient is right; the remainder takes the sign of the number divided, so it is negative.
Two integers divide into an integer; only a float operand keeps the fraction.
Right. −3.4 truncates to −3, and −3 × 5 + (−2) is −17.

prompt: Which of these does the compiler refuse? Choose all that apply.
hint: The compiler can only judge what it can work out before the program runs.

choices.why: Yes: a constant that does not fit is an error, "(overflows)".
Yes: "invalid operation: division by zero", because both operands are constants.
It builds; the division panics when it runs, with exit status 2.
It builds and wraps to −128 at run time, with no message.

prompt: Dividing an integer by a variable that holds zero stops the program with a ___, and it exits with status 2.
hint: The first word the program printed.

prompt: `a, b := 0.1, 0.2` and then `fmt.Println(a+b == 0.3)`. What does it print?
hint: The addition happens at run time, in `float64`.

choices.why: That is what the constant sum gives. In variables the sum is 0.30000000000000004.
Right. Neither 0.1 nor 0.2 is stored exactly, and their sum misses 0.3.

choices.text: Nothing: comparing floats with `==` is a compile error
choices.why: It compiles. That is what makes it dangerous: the compiler allows it, and it is nearly always the wrong test.

choices.text: It panics with a precision error
choices.why: Floats never panic over precision; the result is just a little off.

prompt: Why does `fmt.Println(0.1 + 0.2)` print `0.3`, when the same sum in two variables prints `0.30000000000000004`?
hint: Who does the addition in the first case?

choices.text: The compiler adds the two constants exactly and converts only the result
choices.why: Right. Untyped constants are exact (lesson 5); the rounding happens once, at the end.

choices.text: `Println` rounds every float to one decimal place
choices.why: It printed `0.30000000000000004` for the variables, so it does not round to one place.

choices.text: Go stores literals in decimal and variables in binary
choices.why: A literal that reaches the program is a `float64` like any other; the difference is when the sum is done.
The variable version shows it is not: the `==` with 0.3 was `false`.

prompt: How do you test whether a `float64` called `v` is NaN?
hint: NaN is not equal to anything.

choices.why: That is always `false`, even when `v` is NaN, because NaN is not equal to itself.
That asks about the two infinities. NaN is a different value, and `IsInf` says `false` for it.
Right. It is the test the section used, and it printed `true` for `zero / zero`.
NaN is not a very large number. Every ordering comparison with it is `false`, this one too.

prompt: `zero := 0.0` and then `fmt.Println(1 / zero)`. What happens?
hint: Floats and integers part ways here.

choices.text: It panics: integer divide by zero
choices.why: That panic is for integers. A float division by zero has an answer in IEEE 754.
Right. Positive divided by zero is positive infinity, and the program carries on.
NaN came from `zero / zero`, which has no sensible answer; `1 / zero` has one.
`zero` is a variable, so the compiler cannot know it is zero; only constants are checked.

prompt: A shop adds its prices in `float64`. The screen shows `30.00`, but the check `total == 30.0` fails, so the order is never marked as paid. What is the fix?
hint: What did `%.2f` hide in section 02?

choices.text: Use `float32`, which keeps fewer digits and so rounds the error away
choices.why: Fewer bits make the error larger, not smaller; 0.1 is not exact in either format.

choices.text: Keep every amount as an integer number of cents
choices.why: Right. Integer cents add exactly, and `==` on them means what it says.

choices.text: Add 0.0000001 to the total before comparing
choices.why: The error can fall on either side of 30, so a nudge in one direction fixes some totals and breaks others.

choices.text: Nothing in Go: the prices must have been typed wrong
choices.why: Ten correct prices of 0.10 already gave 0.9999999999999999. The arithmetic, not the input, is off.

prompt: Put the three fields of a `float64` in the order its 64 bits store them, from the first bit printed by `%064b`.
hint: The figure of section 02.

prompt: In the figure, the exponent field of `0.1` holds 1019. The exponent it stands for is 1019 minus 1023. What power of 2 is that?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: What does `math.Sqrt(-1)` return?
hint: `math` works among the real numbers.

choices.why: That is `cmplx.Sqrt(-1)`. The package you call decides which numbers the answer may be.
Right. Among the reals −1 has no square root, so the answer is not a number.

choices.text: It panics, because −1 has no square root
choices.why: Float functions do not panic over an impossible answer; they return NaN and carry on.
No real number squared gives −1, and the function does not return its argument back.

prompt: After `z := complex(3, 4)`, `real(z)` is 3 and `___(z)` is 4.
hint: The built-in that gives the imaginary part.

prompt: Match each literal to the type Go gives it when nothing else says.
hint: The `%T` line of section 01.

prompt: A network protocol puts a port number, 0 to 65535, in two bytes of its header. Which type should the field that holds it have?
hint: The size is part of the meaning, and so is the range.

choices.text: `int16`, because two bytes are sixteen bits
choices.why: Sixteen bits is right, but a signed `int16` stops at 32767, and half the ports would come out negative.
Right. Sixteen bits, no sign, and its range is exactly 0 to 65535.
`int` is the default for counters, and a header field is the case where the size is part of the meaning.
One byte holds 0 to 255; a port needs two.

prompt: `var c uint8 = 200` and then `c += 100`. What does `c` hold?
hint: A `uint8` goes round after 255, and 256 values make one full turn.

choices.why: 300 does not fit in eight bits; the largest `uint8` is 255.

choices.text: `255`, because the value stops at the top
choices.why: Go does not saturate. It wraps, as `127 + 1` did in an `int8`.
Right. 300 − 256 is 44: one full turn of 256 values, and the rest.
`c` is a variable, so the sum is not a constant the compiler can check.
